About: Standing Waves on a String

Source

Topic
Waves — standing waves on a string clamped at both ends
Concept
Drive the string at just any frequency and it thrashes; hit one of its harmonics and the pattern snaps into place with nodes that never move.
Serves
Quantised normal modes, wave speed v = √(T/μ), the standing wave as a superposition of two counter-propagating travelling waves.
Inquiry
Find the lowest locking frequency, then predict the next: just above, twice, or unrelated.
Misconception
"A standing wave is a special kind of wave." It is two ordinary travelling waves going opposite ways, added together.

Guided Inquiry

Step 1 — The apparatus

A string of length L = 1 m is clamped at both ends and shaken at the left end by a shaker running at the drive frequency f. Its tension is T = 100 N and its mass per unit length is μ = 0.01 kg/m, so a transverse wave runs along it at v = √(T/μ) = 100 m/s. The drive frequency, the tension and the mass per unit length can each be changed.

Step 2 — Raising the drive

The drive frequency is raised smoothly from 10 Hz to 250 Hz. How far the string swings changes along the way. Which describes that swing?

Step 3 — The next one up

The lowest frequency the string locks onto is f₁ = 50 Hz. Where is the one after it?

Step 4 — What a standing wave is made of

A standing wave is not a new kind of wave: it is two ordinary travelling waves of the same frequency crossing in opposite directions — the solid blue one sent in by the shaker, the dashed blue one reflected back from the far clamp — added point by point. Where the two always cancel the sum never moves, and that point is a node; midway between two nodes the sum swings hardest, and that point is an antinode.

Step 5 — Tightening the string

The tension is raised from 100 N to 400 N, four times its original value, with the same string. At what frequency does the fundamental now lock?

Step 6 — Everything open

The locks sit at f₁, 2f₁, 3f₁, …, and the nth of them carries n loops, n + 1 nodes and wavelength 2L/n. Tension and mass per unit length move every one of those frequencies together, through v = √(T/μ); they never change the patterns.

The Physics

Standing Waves on a String — the Pattern That Locks · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A string is clamped at both ends and shaken at one end. The sim lets you change the shaking frequency, the tension and the mass of the string, and watch how the string moves. It is the basic model behind every stringed instrument.

What you'll learn

  • How the motion of the string depends on the drive frequency f.
  • How the wave speed v depends on the tension T and the mass per unit length μ.
  • How a pattern on the string is built from two ordinary travelling waves.
  • How to read nodes, antinodes and loops from the picture.
A string of fixed length L = 1 m, clamped at both ends and shaken at the left end.

What's on screen

  • The string: the pink curve between the two fixed ends.
  • The shaker: the teal dot at the left end, moving up and down at the drive frequency.
  • Status chip (bottom): a one-line summary of the string's present state.
  • Readouts (sidebar): the wave speed v and three more numbers for the current drive.
See itOpen the sim at its starting values, with the shaker running. Watch for: the teal shaker dot moving up and down at the left end of the pink string, and the two fixed ends.

03

Fixed ends allow only whole numbers of half-wavelengths

A clamped end cannot move, so each end of the string is a node. A wave sent along the string reflects at the far clamp and comes back. The string swings strongly only when the returning wave arrives in step with the shaker. That happens when a whole number n of half-wavelengths fits into the length:

L = n λ/2    so    fn = n v / (2L),   n = 1, 2, 3, …
Each n is one mode; f₁ is the lowest, called the fundamental.

With the starting values v = 100 m/s and L = 1 m, so f₁ = 50 Hz and the modes sit at 50, 100, 150, 200 Hz and so on. They are whole-number multiples of f₁, with nothing in between. The n-th mode has n loops of the string, and a wavelength λ = 2L/n.

See itSet the drive to 50 Hz, with T = 100 N and μ = 0.01 kg/m. Watch for: one big loop of the string, with the chip reading n = 1 • 1 loop, 2 nodes • f₁ = 50.0 Hz.
04

Tension and density set the speed, and the speed sets every frequency

The speed of a transverse wave on the string depends only on the string:

v = √(T / μ)
T in newtons, μ in kg per metre, v in m/s.

Every fn = n v/(2L) is proportional to v, so all the frequencies move together by the same factor. The shapes do not change: mode n always has n loops.

  • Tension is under a square root. Quadrupling T doubles v: T = 400 N gives v = 200 m/s and f₁ = 100 Hz.
  • A heavier string is slower. Quadrupling μ halves v: μ = 0.04 kg/m with T = 100 N gives v = 50 m/s and f₁ = 25 Hz, f₂ = 50 Hz.
See itRaise the tension to 400 N and set the drive to 100 Hz. Watch for: the string locked in one loop at 100 Hz, and the readout v = 200.0 m/s.
05

A standing wave is two travelling waves added together

A standing wave is not a new kind of wave. The shaker sends a wave to the right, and the far clamp reflects an equal wave to the left. Adding them point by point gives

A sin(kx − ωt) + A sin(kx + ωt) = 2A sin(kx) cos(ωt)
The factor sin(kx) fixes the shape; cos(ωt) only makes it breathe up and down.

Where sin(kx) = 0 the two waves always cancel: a node, at x = kL/n for k = 0, 1, …, n. Midway between two nodes the swing is largest, 2A: an antinode. So the n-th mode has n loops, n antinodes and n + 1 nodes, counting the two ends.

See itSet the drive to 150 Hz, with T = 100 N and μ = 0.01 kg/m. Watch for: 4 amber node dots and 3 loops, with the two faint blue travelling waves drawn beneath the pink string.
06

Between the modes the string barely responds

You can shake the string at any frequency. Off a mode, the reflected wave comes back out of step with the shaker, so the two travelling waves do not line up. Their sum does not hold still and the swing stays small.

A real string loses a little energy each cycle, so a resonance has a finite width. This sim gives each mode a half-width of 2.5 Hz: if the drive is Δf away from the nearest mode, the swing is a fraction 1/√(1 + (Δf/2.5 Hz)²) of the full one.

  • Δf = 0.6 Hz: 97%. The sim calls the string locked within 0.6 Hz of a mode.
  • Δf = 2.5 Hz: 71%.
  • Δf = 10 Hz: 24%. Δf = 20 Hz: 12%, which is where the sim opens at 30 Hz.
See itSet the drive to 40 Hz, 10 Hz below f₁ = 50 Hz. Watch for: the chip off resonance with Δf = -10.0 Hz, and a swing of about a quarter of the f₁ swing.
07

Where it matters

  • Tuning. The peg on a guitar or violin sets the tension T. Raising T raises v, and with it every frequency the string can sound.
  • String choice. Thicker, heavier strings (larger μ) sound lower. Bass strings on a piano are wound with wire to add mass without making the string much stiffer.
  • Fretting. Pressing a string against a fret shortens L, which raises fn = n v/(2L). This sim keeps L fixed at 1 m.
  • Tone. A plucked string sounds several modes at once, f₁, 2f₁, 3f₁, …. The mix of them is what makes a guitar and a violin sound different on the same note.
08

Summary

In one line. How a clamped string answers a shaker is set by its length L, its tension T, its mass per unit length μ and the drive frequency f.

Key points

  • v = √(T/μ), and the modes are fn = n v/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3, …
  • The n-th mode has n loops, n + 1 nodes and wavelength 2L/n.
  • A standing wave is two equal travelling waves crossing in opposite directions.

Common mix-ups

  • "A standing wave is a special kind of wave." It is two ordinary travelling waves added together.
  • "Off a mode, the string does not move." It moves, but only by a small fraction of the full swing.
  • "More tension changes the pattern on the string." It moves every frequency by the same factor. Mode n still has n loops.

Things to try on your own

  • With T = 100 N and μ = 0.01 kg/m, find the drive that gives 4 loops, then count the nodes.
  • Find the lowest f₁ the sliders allow, and the T and μ that give it.
  • Pick any T and μ, work out f₃ yourself, then set the drive to it and compare the chip.
